name: Baby
baseMeaning: A picture of a bundled infant with a round face, a curl of hair and a pacifier. Read in a message it lands as cooing over something small and new.
tldr: 👶 Baby. In a chat it comes across as cooing over something small and new.

contextMeanings.meaning: The plain reading: a bundled infant with a round face, a curl of hair and a pacifier. Nothing hidden in the drawing itself.
contextMeanings.example: Reacting to a newborn photo in a family chat 👶

contextMeanings.meaning: Borrowed as a reaction, it reads as cooing over something small and new.
contextMeanings.example: Calling a friend's new puppy a tiny human 👶

contextMeanings.meaning: In a dating thread the gesture is usually doing the work of a line that was not typed. It arrives as cooing over something small and new, softened by whatever sentence sits next to it.

In a work channel it is read the same way it is read anywhere else — cooing over something small and new — but the stakes of a misread are higher, because the sender is often talking about somebody's actual work.

platformNotes.note: In Slack 👶 lands in channels where the sentence was supposed to be shorter. It is usually standing in for reacting to a newborn photo in a family chat, and a channel where the topic is somebody's workload is where it misreads.
On Discord 👶 is a staple of the reaction bar, which is why it so often arrives stripped of its cooing over something small and new reading — a shape pressed rather than a message sent.

On X and Twitter 👶 does most of its work in replies, where it tags a message like calling a friend's new puppy a tiny human. Short enough to survive being the whole post, which is exactly why it is used that way.

On iOS the Baby 👶 renders as the neutral drawing, and the neutral swatch is what most people send without thinking about it. A message like reacting to a newborn photo in a family chat is the kind that carries it — the picture lands before the sentence does.

WhatsApp renders 👶 exactly as the phone system does, but the keyboard keeps it in the person section, where nobody looks unless they are hunting for it. In family threads it tends to accompany a message like calling a friend's new puppy a tiny human.

generationalNotes.note: Gen Z reaches for 👶 to do the work of reacting to a newborn photo in a family chat, and treats the neutral drawing as the default rather than as a choice. What they hear first is cooing over something small and new.

Millennials tend to send 👶 deliberately, usually for something like calling a friend's new puppy a tiny human, and they read cooing over something small and new into it more often than the older cohorts do.
Gen X mostly uses 👶 literally, as the picture of the gesture itself, and is less likely to read cooing over something small and new into it than younger senders are.
Older senders use 👶 in the most straightforward way, on family and group messages, and are less likely to hear the cooing over something small and new subtext in it.

warnings.title: 👶 and 🍼 get swapped
warnings.description: The Baby Bottle 🍼 is one tap away in every picker, and it does not carry the same reading — the bottle stands in for the caregiving act, the baby stands in for the small new thing itself. Check which one you actually picked.

warnings.title: The reading it usually gets is not the one it was sent with
warnings.description: People take 👶 as something else fairly often: it gets assumed to be a literal infant when it is most often a stand-in for whatever the sender is fussing over, because the pacifier makes it read as sweet rather than specific. The sentence around it is usually what settles the meaning.

seoTitle: 👶 Baby Emoji - What It Actually Means in Text
seoDescription: 👶 Baby meaning: cooing over something small and new. How the emoji is used at work, at home and in dating threads, and where it goes wrong.

longForm.overview:
The drawing of 👶 is a bundled infant with a round face, a curl of hair and a pacifier. It arrived with Unicode 13.0 in the person section, and in a conversation it does the work of a line somebody left out on purpose.

The line it stands in for is cooing over something small and new. That is the reading most people arrive with, and it is usually the intended one — a picture carries the same meaning as the sentence it replaces, and it arrives first.

The complication is that the drawing invites a second reading. It gets assumed to be a literal infant when it is most often a stand-in for whatever the sender is fussing over, because the pacifier makes it read as sweet rather than specific. In practice that second reading is not rare — it is the one that decides how a message lands, because the sender has usually not thought about it at all.

It also sits in the crowded part of the picker. The nearest neighbour is 🍼 Baby Bottle: the bottle stands in for the caregiving act, the baby stands in for the small new thing itself. The two are close enough that a fast thumb picks the wrong one, and the message goes out carrying a meaning nobody chose.

The baby also exists in five skin tones. They are separate pages with separate copy, because picking a tone is a decision in a way that picking the plain emoji is not: it says something about who the sender thinks the reader is.

In short — the baby reads as cooing over something small and new, it is most often used for reacting to a newborn photo in a family chat or calling a friend's new puppy a tiny human, and the five tone pages under it each say something different about who is sending it. The rest of the page takes those three apart.
longForm.howPeopleUseIt:
Context, not the picture, decides how this lands. 👶 in a work thread is calling a friend's new puppy a tiny human; 👶 in a family thread is reacting to a newborn photo in a family chat; 👶 in a thread with somebody you like is a way of saying something you would rather not type out.

The tone versions of the emoji make the same point from the other side. The gesture is identical in all five, and the swatch says something about the sender before a word is read.

The shortest messages are the risky ones. A lone 👶 is the whole reply, and it is carrying a meaning nobody wrote down — cooing over something small and new is the intention, but what arrives is a drawing. Everything the sentence would have disambiguated is simply missing.

Put it this way. Reacting to a newborn photo in a family chat is the job the baby does most: it saves a sentence and lands faster than one would have. Calling a friend's new puppy a tiny human is the job it does second: there the picture is not the point, it is the temperature of the message.
longForm.whenNotToUse:
Think about what the emoji is replacing. If the sentence under it is doing the real work, 👶 will get assumed to be a literal infant when it is most often a stand-in for whatever the sender is fussing over, because the pacifier makes it read as sweet rather than specific instead, and the thread ends up carrying a meaning nobody wrote.

And keep it away from first contact. There is nothing warm in the drawing, and a baby gesture used to answer other people's messages tends to sound like it is settling a point.

Keep it out of the formal register. In a thread about somebody's work, or in a message to somebody you have not met, 👶 reads as cooing over something small and new, and formality is exactly where that reading does the most damage.

Leave 🍼 Baby Bottle for the other message. The bottle stands in for the caregiving act, the baby stands in for the small new thing itself. And keep 👶 out of threads where somebody is hurting: it reads as cooing over something small and new there, because there is nothing in the drawing that says you meant well.
longForm.howToReply:
The safe move in an unclear thread is to answer the text. 👶 gets assumed to be a literal infant when it is most often a stand-in for whatever the sender is fussing over, because the pacifier makes it read as sweet rather than specific often enough that the sentence matters more than the picture.

And do not send 👶 alone when the message underneath is supposed to be warm. A message like reacting to a newborn photo in a family chat carries the feeling; the picture on its own leaves the reader choosing between cooing over something small and new and something sharper.

Start by reading what the 👶 was doing. If it was a reaction, react: 👶 back, and the thread is closed. If it was aimed at you, write. The difference matters, because the reply to a reaction can be a picture and the reply to a request cannot.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 👶 and its skin-tone versions?
faqs.answer: The tone variants under baby show the same gesture in five different skin tones. The gesture does not change, but the tone is a small signal about who the sender imagines the reader is, and in some groups that signal is read louder than the sentence.

faqs.question: What does 👶 mean in text?
faqs.answer: 👶 is used for cooing over something small and new. The drawing shows a bundled infant with a round face, a curl of hair and a pacifier, and that part is not in dispute — what changes is whether the sender is being literal or borrowing the gesture for a reaction.

faqs.question: What is the difference between 👶 and 🍼?
faqs.answer: The bottle stands in for the caregiving act, the baby stands in for the small new thing itself. The two sit close together in most pickers, so the difference is often about which one the sender pressed rather than about what they meant.

faqs.question: Is 👶 rude?
faqs.answer: It can be. The gesture is meant as cooing over something small and new, but it gets assumed to be a literal infant when it is most often a stand-in for whatever the sender is fussing over, because the pacifier makes it read as sweet rather than specific. The risk is highest when it is the only message in the thread — a sentence gives the picture some context to sit in.

faqs.question: What does 👶 mean from a guy?
faqs.answer: Nothing gender-specific. The same reading applies whoever sends it, and the meaning is set by the thread and by what is written next to it rather than by the sender.

conversationExamples.interpretation: A public sign-off, with the emoji as the full stop. The picture is doing the punctuation, which is why it is sent instead of a sentence.

conversationExamples.message: reacting to a newborn photo in a family chat 👶
conversationExamples.interpretation: The everyday use: the picture carries the whole line. It lands as cooing over something small and new, and matching it with the same emoji is a normal reply.

conversationExamples.message: calling a friend's new puppy a tiny human 👶
conversationExamples.interpretation: A handover or a sign-off in a channel. It reads as cooing over something small and new, and naming the next step in words is usually clearer than leaving it to the gesture.

conversationExamples.message: there is something you should know 👶
conversationExamples.interpretation: A small joke or a nudge, with the emoji doing the tone work. It gets assumed to be a literal infant when it is most often a stand-in for whatever the sender is fussing over, because the pacifier makes it read as sweet rather than specific more easily here than it does in a work thread, because the thread is thinner.

conversationExamples.message: reacting to a newborn photo in a family chat 👶
conversationExamples.interpretation: Family threads are where this lands most naturally. The reading is cooing over something small and new, and nobody in the thread is reading it as anything sharper than that.
